CANDIDATE_SHA256: 390abf8fb7b61ffb6a1e495a1df0985ae770d3f19a979cc4bffccdb0f66eedaf

I reviewed the full file at `artifacts/editorial/release-candidates/technology/windows-11-july-update-pause-restore-controls.mdx`, its research artifact, the prior review artifact, the promoted copy in `content/technology/`, and the image on disk. The article's readable content needs no correction before publication. One integrity caveat is noted below that you should be aware of, though it does not stem from the article text itself.

**Hash verification caveat (important, but not a content defect).** My tools this session (Read/Grep/Glob only, no shell) cannot recompute SHA-256, so I could not independently confirm the supplied hash. Notably, the repository's own records — the prior review artifact (`...a04205a69817.json`), the learning log, and the promoted file's `candidateSha256` frontmatter — all record a **different** hash for this same candidate path: `a04205a698...`. That means either the file's bytes changed after the earlier review (e.g., line-ending normalization on this Windows checkout) or the two hashes were computed on different encodings. I verified the candidate's readable content is line-for-line identical to the already-published copy in `content/technology/` (the only differences are the expected frontmatter fields: `status`, review/promotion metadata). My verdict applies to the file as it exists at that path right now.

**Factual support and source use.** Every load-bearing claim is explicitly attributed to Microsoft and tied to one of four primary Microsoft URLs matching the research artifact exactly. Independently checkable facts hold up: builds 26200/26100 correspond to 25H2/24H2; the 35-day pause ceiling matches Windows Update's long-standing five-week maximum; the Windows 11 24H2 Home/Pro end-of-servicing date of October 13, 2026 is correct (24 months from the October 2024 GA); and the point-in-time restore behavior (VSS-based, ~24-hour capture, ~72-hour retention, includes user files, BitLocker recovery-key path, default-on for unmanaged Home/Pro with a 200 GB+ OS volume) matches Microsoft's documentation of the feature announced in late 2025. Post-cutoff specifics (the .8875 revision, the July 15 amendment, the Dell/Intel IPF hold) are consistently framed as "Microsoft says" and rest on the cited KB and Learn pages rather than being asserted independently — the correct posture.

**Unsupported claims.** None found. The piece is careful to bound its own advice: pause is "not a security strategy," restore "does not make updates risk-free" and is "not a long archive."

**Title/meta, structure, usefulness.** Title, subtitle, and description accurately reflect the body with no clickbait. The structure (framing intro, four sourced H2 sections, consolidated Sources block) directly serves the stated reader job of install/pause/wait. Cosmetic nit only: the final section lacks the `---` separator before `## Sources` that the other sections have.

**Image and frontmatter integrity.** The image exists at the referenced path; I viewed it and it matches the alt text — abstract update/calendar/pause/shield icons with no readable text, so no fake-UI risk — and the attribution honestly discloses it as generated. Slug matches filename, category matches directory, `status: release-candidate` is correct for this path, and "4 min read" fits the ~830-word length.

**Reputational/legal risk.** Low. Dell and Intel appear only via Microsoft's own compatibility notice, the article never advises skipping security updates, and there are no disparagement or warranty-adjacent claims.

Two non-blocking follow-ups for the publish pipeline: reconcile the hash discrepancy against the repository's recorded `a04205a6...` value so the chain of custody is unambiguous, and spot-check the pause-updates URL (`support.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/deployment/updates-lifecycle/...` has a learn.microsoft.com-style path on the support domain) against the live site.
